screens.title: Iteration: for and while Loops
screens.narratorSegment: Iteration is one of the most practical tools you will use in programming. When you have many items to process, or a condition that must be checked repeatedly, loops let your program perform the same steps without manual repetition. In Python, the two main loop styles are the for loop, which walks through an iterable like a list or a range of numbers, and the while loop, which repeats as long as a condition stays true. Both solve real problems: from emailing a thousand customers to polling input until valid data arrives. You will also learn how to steer loops using break and continue, and how the loop else clause can tell you whether a search completed normally. Finally, we’ll address common errors — infinite loops and off-by-one mistakes — and show safe patterns for modifying data while iterating. By the end of this chapter, you’ll be able to pick the right loop type, write concise loop logic, and avoid the usual pitfalls when automating repeated tasks. Consider a simple task now: counting valid temperature readings from a list. That kind of task becomes short and readable with a loop. How would you decide which loop to use when you start a problem?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Iteration Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Why loops matter

Loops let you scale actions from single steps to thousands of items and keep logic compact and clear.

screens.title: What is iteration?
screens.narratorSegment: Iteration means repeating a block of code multiple times so you can handle many tasks with the same instructions. Think of a bakery where the baker follows the same steps for each loaf: mix, knead, bake. In programming, a loop applies the same set of steps to each item in a collection or repeats until a condition changes. This saves effort and reduces errors because you write the logic once and apply it consistently. Practically, iteration is used whenever you process lists of data, produce repeated output, or run checks until a particular state is reached. A common misconception is that loops must only handle lists; in fact, some loops run until an external condition changes, like user input or reaching a maximum attempt count. Another misconception is that loops always improve speed; they improve code expressiveness and maintainability, but algorithmic complexity still matters. For example, you can use a loop to scan a log file line by line, to compute an average across thousands of readings, or to prompt a user until valid input is provided. A closing question to consider: when you see repeated statements in your code, could a loop make it shorter and safer?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Iteration repeats a code block for each item or until a condition changes, enabling scalable and consistent processing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is iteration?
Definition

Iteration explained

Repeat the same steps reliably for multiple items or until a condition changes. This improves readability and reduces duplication.

Analogy

A bakery repeating the same recipe for each loaf is like a loop applying the same code to each item.

Common use cases
  • Processing records in a list or file
  • Aggregating values like sums or averages
  • Prompting users until valid input arrives
Example

Counting valid items

A loop can scan readings and collect valid ones into a new list while skipping invalid markers.

# Example pattern (conceptual)
readings = [25.5, -999, 26.1]
valid = []
for r in readings:
  if r == -999:
    continue
  valid.append(r)
# valid now holds only non-marker values
Key Takeaway

When you see repeated actions, prefer a loop. Decide whether you know the number of iterations or must loop until a condition changes.

screens.title: for loops and iterables
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop takes each element from an iterable and runs the loop body for that element. Iterables include lists, tuples, strings, sets, and dictionaries. When you write a for loop, you choose a loop variable name that represents each item as the loop runs. For example, when iterating over a list of names, the loop variable will take one name at a time and you can act on it. A common pattern is to build a new list of processed items rather than mutating the list you are iterating over; modifying a list while iterating can produce surprising results. The range function is often used with for when you need numeric indices or a fixed count. A misconception is that for cannot be used to count; in fact, range provides numbers for counting. Concrete example: given a list of temperatures, you can iterate with for to skip invalid markers and count high readings. Practice will show that clear naming and small loop bodies make for loops easy to reason about. Consider when you would iterate over keys, values, or both when working with dictionaries.

keyIdea.title: for loop use

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › for loops
Code walkthrough

Iterating a collection

Use descriptive loop variables and avoid mutating the iterable while iterating.

temperatures = [25.5, 27.0, -999, 26.1]
valid_temperatures = []
for temp in temperatures:
  if temp == -999:
    continue
  valid_temperatures.append(temp)
# valid_temperatures now contains only valid readings
Tip
Iterate over a copy if you must remove items from a list during traversal.
Misconception
Altering the list while iterating can skip items or cause unexpected behavior.
Use case

Filtering and transforming

Use for loops to build new lists of cleaned or converted values, which keeps original data intact for verification.

Key Takeaway

For loops visit each element of an iterable. Keep loop bodies focused and avoid in-place removals when possible.

Visual
Iterable examples
  • String → characters
  • List → items in order
  • Dictionary → iterate keys or items()
When to use for

When you can enumerate every item or when you need a fixed number of iterations using range.

screens.title: range() and off-by-one errors
screens.narratorSegment: The range function generates a sequence of numbers and is a common partner for for loops. Its forms include range(stop), range(start, stop), and range(start, stop, step). A vital detail to remember is that the stop value is excluded — range(5) produces numbers from zero to four. That exclusion is the source of many off-by-one errors when beginners expect the stop to be included. Off-by-one mistakes can make loops run one time too many or one time too few, causing incorrect counts or index errors. To avoid this, think in terms of half-open intervals: start is included, stop is excluded. Use clear naming and test small ranges to confirm behavior. The step parameter can generate descending sequences when negative, but ensure start and stop align with the step sign. A practical example is iterating over indices for a list: use range(len(list)) when you need indices. A quick check: print the list of numbers that range will produce for the arguments you plan to use before applying the loop logic. range() and off-by-one errors means range excludes its stop value. treat ranges as half-open intervals to avoid off-by-one bugs.. In practical terms, using range(start, stop, step) and avoiding common boundary mistakes.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: range excludes its stop value. Treat ranges as half-open intervals to avoid off-by-one bugs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › range() and boundaries
Reference

How range works

Remember: range produces numbers from start up to but not including stop. This half-open interval is intentional and consistent across Python.

# Examples
list(range(5))        # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
list(range(1, 5))     # [1, 2, 3, 4]
list(range(5, 0, -1)) # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
Pitfall
Assuming range(stop) includes stop leads to missed or extra iterations.
Check
Print the sequence from range during development to confirm it matches expectations.
Example

Indexing a list

When you need indexes, iterate over range(len(my_list)) and be careful with stop value to cover valid indexes only.

Key Takeaway

Think of range as start <= value < stop. Use small tests to confirm boundary behavior before using indices in logic.

Visual check
Half-open interval

Range includes the start and excludes the stop. This rule prevents off-by-one surprises when applied consistently.

Quick rule

If you need N iterations, use range(N) and remember the last value is N-1.

screens.title: while loops and infinite loops
screens.narratorSegment: while loops repeat a block as long as a condition stays true. This makes them ideal when you do not know the exact number of iterations in advance, for example when waiting for valid user input or processing until a sentinel value appears. The critical safety rule is to ensure the condition will eventually become false. A common cause of infinite loops is failing to update the variable used in the loop condition. Another cause is a logic path that always leaves the condition unchanged. To prevent infinite loops, include statements that advance counters, change flags, or break after a maximum number of attempts. Use a maximum attempts pattern when interacting with users, as in prompting for a password with a limited number of tries. Also test the loop with small datasets and deliberate invalid input to confirm that termination occurs. When in doubt, add a clear progress update or a final else clause to document normal completion. keyIdea.title: while safety
keyIdea.text: Ensure loop conditions are updated so the loop will terminate; use counters or limits to avoid infinite execution.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › while loops
Definition

Indefinite repetition

Use while when the termination depends on a runtime condition instead of a known number of steps.

# Example: limited login attempts
attempts = 0
max_attempts = 3
password = ""
while password != "secret" and attempts < max_attempts:
  password = input("Enter password: ")
  if password == "secret":
    print("Access granted")
  else:
    print("Incorrect")
  attempts += 1
else:
  if password != "secret":
    print("Too many failed attempts")
Common mistake
Not changing a condition variable inside the loop produces an infinite loop.
Pro-tip
Use a counter or a clear break condition in interactive loops to ensure termination.
When to pick while

Choose while when the number of iterations depends on user input, external events, or dynamic state changes.

Key Takeaway

Design the loop so a clearly defined variable or condition will progress toward termination on every iteration.

Safety checks
Checklist
  • Is the loop condition well-defined?
  • Does something in the body change that condition?
  • Do you have a fallback or counter to break after many attempts?
Misconception

Loops are safe by default; in reality, you must design for termination explicitly.

screens.title: break and continue
screens.narratorSegment: break and continue let you control how a loop proceeds. The break statement immediately exits the nearest loop, which is useful when you are searching for a target and can stop once it is found. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next item, useful when you want to ignore certain values but keep looping. A frequent pattern combines both: skip invalid data with continue, and break when a success condition occurs. One misconception is that continue affects outer loops; it only advances the current loop. Another is assuming break will also skip the else clause — in fact, if break occurs, the loop's else block will not run, and that distinction is handy for search logic. A concrete example is searching a list of numbers for the first even value; when found, break stops further checks. When using nested loops, be explicit about which loop you intend to exit; break only exits the innermost loop by default. Practice combining break and else to implement clean search patterns that either report a found item or run fallback code when nothing is found.

keyIdea.title: Flow control
keyIdea.text: Use break to stop a loop early and continue to skip a single iteration; remember break prevents the loop else clause from running.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › break & continue
Process Flow

Stop or skip

break exits the loop immediately. continue skips to the next iteration. Use both to keep loop logic small and explicit.

numbers = [1, 3, 5, 8, 9]
for n in numbers:
  if n < 0:
    continue  # skip negatives
  if n % 2 == 0:
    print(f"First even number found: {n}")
    break
else:
  print("No even numbers found")
Pattern
Use continue to filter, break to short-circuit a search, and else to handle the not-found case.
Watch out
break prevents the loop's else block from executing, which matters in search patterns.
Analogy

Think of continue as skipping a single tray on a conveyor, and break as stopping the conveyor entirely when you find what you need.

Key Takeaway

Use continue to keep loop bodies focused, and break to stop work early when a result is found. Combine with else for clear search outcomes.

Example flow
Search pattern

Iterate and break when found. Use else to run code if nothing was found.

Filter pattern

Skip invalid items with continue and continue processing the rest of the list.

screens.title: The loop else clause
screens.narratorSegment: Python's loop else clause runs only when the loop finishes normally, that is, when it iterates through all items or the while condition becomes false. If a break occurs, the else block is skipped. This makes else useful for search operations: you can report a found item inside the loop and use else to report a not-found outcome without setting a separate flag. A common misconception is that else pairs with break or acts like an error handler; instead, else simply signals a normal completion. Use else sparingly for clarity: it reads well when you implement a search that either finds a target with break or reaches the end and runs else. For example, iterate through a list looking for a matching value and break when you find it; if you never find it, use else to print a not-found message. This pattern avoids additional state variables and keeps the search logic concise. As a closure, ask yourself whether your code will be clearer with a simple flag and if-else, or with the loop else clause. The loop else clause means the else block executes only when a loop completes without break — handy for search completion logic without extra flags.. In practical terms, how else works with for and while and when to use it.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loop else
keyIdea.text: The else block executes only when a loop completes without break — handy for search completion logic without extra flags.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Loop else clause
Definition

When else runs

Else runs after normal completion of a loop. If a break happens, else is skipped. Use this to differentiate found versus not-found results.

for x in items:
  if match(x):
    print("Found")
    break
else:
  print("Not found")

# The else runs only if break never executed
When to use
Search operations and verification steps where a normal finish needs handling.
Avoid
Overusing else when a simple boolean flag would be clearer to new readers.
Example

Iterate through a list to find an even number; print the found value and break. If none are found, else prints a not-found message. This keeps the code compact.

Key Takeaway

Use loop else to express 'nothing found' outcomes without extra state variables. Remember break prevents else from running.

Analogy
Library search

Search shelves; break when you find the book. If you finish the shelf without finding it, else handles the not-found result.

Clarity tip

Use else only when it improves readability; otherwise a flag or separate check is fine.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging loops
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding common loop mistakes will make your code more robust. Infinite loops occur when the loop condition never becomes false; the fix is to ensure some state inside the loop moves toward termination, such as incrementing a counter or reading new input. Off-by-one errors often stem from misunderstanding range boundaries; check whether your start and stop values include the elements you expect. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Temperature processing
Code walkthrough

Filter, count, aggregate

temperatures = [25.5, 27.0, 24.8, -999, 26.1, 28.3, -999, 25.9]
valid_temperatures = []
high_temp_threshold = 28.0
high_temp_count = 0
invalid_marker = -999

for temp in temperatures:
  if temp == invalid_marker:
    print(f"Skipping invalid reading: {temp}")
    continue
  valid_temperatures.append(temp)
  if temp > high_temp_threshold:
    high_temp_count += 1
    print(f"High temperature detected: {temp}°C")

# Average calculation
if valid_temperatures:
  total = 0
  for t in valid_temperatures:
    total += t
  average_temp = total / len(valid_temperatures)
  print(f"Average valid temperature: {average_temp:.2f}°C")
else:
  print("No valid temperatures to calculate average.")
Why this pattern

Separating filtering and aggregation keeps logic clear and avoids index mistakes. The first pass cleans data; the second computes aggregates safely.

Key Takeaway

Use continue to skip invalid markers, collect valid items, and always check for emptiness before dividing to avoid runtime errors.

Scenario

Sensors may emit invalid markers. A robust program filters these markers out and only analyzes valid readings to compute reliable statistics.

Try this

Change the invalid marker and threshold, then re-run the code to see how results update.

Misconception

Calculating average on the original list without removing markers may yield incorrect averages or runtime errors.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Recall Cards
Range rule

If you need N iterations, use range(N) and expect the last value to be N-1.

Progress

Always change a loop condition inside a while loop or provide a maximum attempts guard to prevent infinite runs.

Mutation

Avoid removing or inserting items in the list you are iterating; iterate a copy or build a new list instead.

Closing thought

Small habits around range boundaries, termination progress, and safe mutation make loops predictable and easy to test.

fullNarratorScript:
Iteration is one of the most practical tools you will use in programming. When you have many items to process, or a condition that must be checked repeatedly, loops let your program perform the same steps without manual repetition. In Python, the two main loop styles are the for loop, which walks through an iterable like a list or a range of numbers, and the while loop, which repeats as long as a condition stays true. Both solve real problems: from emailing a thousand customers to polling input until valid data arrives. You will also learn how to steer loops using break and continue, and how the loop else clause can tell you whether a search completed normally. Finally, we’ll address common errors — infinite loops and off-by-one mistakes — and show safe patterns for modifying data while iterating. By the end of this chapter, you’ll be able to pick the right loop type, write concise loop logic, and avoid the usual pitfalls when automating repeated tasks. Consider a simple task now: counting valid temperature readings from a list. That kind of task becomes short and readable with a loop. How would you decide which loop to use when you start a problem?

Over the next screens you will build a clear mental model of looping in Python and practical skills you can use immediately. First, you will learn what iteration means and why it is a fundamental tool for processing collections and repeating tasks. Next, you will implement for loops to walk through iterables and use the range function for counting and indexing. You will also implement while loops for situations where the number of repetitions is not known ahead of time, like prompting for valid input. Along the way we will practice using break to stop a search early and continue to skip unwanted items. You will study the loop else clause and how it signals a normal completion, then learn to identify common errors such as infinite loops and off-by-one indexing mistakes. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check your progress and apply loops safely in real tasks.

We build on the basic objectives with practical habits you need for robust code. First, you will master the range function so you can count, index, and generate numeric sequences reliably; remember that range excludes its stop value, which is a common source of off-by-one mistakes. Second, you will practice using the loop else clause in search patterns to detect when nothing was found without extra flags. Third, you will learn how to detect and prevent infinite loops by changing loop conditions in the body, using counters or user responses. Finally, you will practice applying loops to real data tasks, such as filtering temperature readings and counting threshold exceedances. Each objective pairs an explanation with a small mnemonic and a verified milestone so you can check that your loops behave correctly in tests and examples.

Iteration means repeating a block of code multiple times so you can handle many tasks with the same instructions. Think of a bakery where the baker follows the same steps for each loaf: mix, knead, bake. In programming, a loop applies the same set of steps to each item in a collection or repeats until a condition changes. This saves effort and reduces errors because you write the logic once and apply it consistently. Practically, iteration is used whenever you process lists of data, produce repeated output, or run checks until a particular state is reached. A common misconception is that loops must only handle lists; in fact, some loops run until an external condition changes, like user input or reaching a maximum attempt count. Another misconception is that loops always improve speed; they improve code expressiveness and maintainability, but algorithmic complexity still matters. For example, you can use a loop to scan a log file line by line, to compute an average across thousands of readings, or to prompt a user until valid input is provided. A closing question to consider: when you see repeated statements in your code, could a loop make it shorter and safer?

A for loop takes each element from an iterable and runs the loop body for that element. Iterables include lists, tuples, strings, sets, and dictionaries. When you write a for loop, you choose a loop variable name that represents each item as the loop runs. For example, when iterating over a list of names, the loop variable will take one name at a time and you can act on it. A common pattern is to build a new list of processed items rather than mutating the list you are iterating over; modifying a list while iterating can produce surprising results. The range function is often used with for when you need numeric indices or a fixed count. A misconception is that for cannot be used to count; in fact, range provides numbers for counting. Concrete example: given a list of temperatures, you can iterate with for to skip invalid markers and count high readings. Practice will show that clear naming and small loop bodies make for loops easy to reason about. Consider when you would iterate over keys, values, or both when working with dictionaries.

The range function generates a sequence of numbers and is a common partner for for loops. Its forms include range(stop), range(start, stop), and range(start, stop, step). A vital detail to remember is that the stop value is excluded — range(5) produces numbers from zero to four. That exclusion is the source of many off-by-one errors when beginners expect the stop to be included. Off-by-one mistakes can make loops run one time too many or one time too few, causing incorrect counts or index errors. To avoid this, think in terms of half-open intervals: start is included, stop is excluded. Use clear naming and test small ranges to confirm behavior. The step parameter can generate descending sequences when negative, but ensure start and stop align with the step sign. A practical example is iterating over indices for a list: use range(len(list)) when you need indices. A quick check: print the list of numbers that range will produce for the arguments you plan to use before applying the loop logic. range() and off-by-one errors means range excludes its stop value. treat ranges as half-open intervals to avoid off-by-one bugs.. while loops repeat a block as long as a condition stays true. This makes them ideal when you do not know the exact number of iterations in advance, for example when waiting for valid user input or processing until a sentinel value appears. The critical safety rule is to ensure the condition will eventually become false. A common cause of infinite loops is failing to update the variable used in the loop condition. Another cause is a logic path that always leaves the condition unchanged. To prevent infinite loops, include statements that advance counters, change flags, or break after a maximum number of attempts. Use a maximum attempts pattern when interacting with users, as in prompting for a password with a limited number of tries. break and continue let you control how a loop proceeds. The break statement immediately exits the nearest loop, which is useful when you are searching for a target and can stop once it is found. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next item, useful when you want to ignore certain values but keep looping. A frequent pattern combines both: skip invalid data with continue, and break when a success condition occurs. One misconception is that continue affects outer loops; it only advances the current loop. Another is assuming break will also skip the else clause — in fact, if break occurs, the loop's else block will not run, and that distinction is handy for search logic. A concrete example is searching a list of numbers for the first even value; when found, break stops further checks. When using nested loops, be explicit about which loop you intend to exit; break only exits the innermost loop by default. Practice combining break and else to implement clean search patterns that either report a found item or run fallback code when nothing is found.

Python's loop else clause runs only when the loop finishes normally, that is, when it iterates through all items or the while condition becomes false. If a break occurs, the else block is skipped. This makes else useful for search operations: you can report a found item inside the loop and use else to report a not-found outcome without setting a separate flag. A common misconception is that else pairs with break or acts like an error handler; instead, else simply signals a normal completion. Use else sparingly for clarity: it reads well when you implement a search that either finds a target with break or reaches the end and runs else. For example, iterate through a list looking for a matching value and break when you find it; if you never find it, use else to print a not-found message. This pattern avoids additional state variables and keeps the search logic concise. As a closure, ask yourself whether your code will be clearer with a simple flag and if-else, or with the loop else clause.
